title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 34
paragraphs: Pierre ran through various yards and side streets with his small burden and got back to the Gruzinski garden at the corner of the Povarskoy. At first he did not recognize the place he had set out from to look for the child. He could not, because it was now so crowded with people and with goods dragged out of the houses. Russian families had taken refuge there from the fire with their belongings, and among them were several French soldiers in assorted clothing. Pierre paid them no attention. He hurried to find the civil servant's family, so he could give the daughter back to her mother and go off to save someone else. Pierre felt he still had a great deal to do, and had to do it fast. He was flushed from the heat and the running, and at that moment he felt more strongly than ever the youth, vitality and resolve that had come over him when he ran to save the child. She had gone quiet now. She clung to Pierre's coat with her little hands and sat on his arm looking around her like a small wild animal. He glanced at her now and then with a faint smile. He thought he saw something touchingly innocent in that frightened, sickly little face.

He did not find the civil servant or his wife where he had left them. He walked quickly through the crowd, scanning the faces he passed. Without meaning to, he noticed a Georgian or Armenian family: a very handsome old man of Oriental type in a new, cloth-covered sheepskin coat and new boots, an old woman of the same type, and a young woman. To Pierre this young woman seemed the perfection of Oriental beauty. Her black eyebrows were sharply drawn and arched, and her long, lovely, expressionless face had an extraordinarily soft, bright color. Amid the scattered belongings and the crowd on the open ground, she wore a rich satin cloak and a bright lilac shawl on her head, and she looked like a delicate exotic plant thrown out onto the snow. She sat on some bundles a little behind the old woman. From under her long lashes she gazed at the ground in front of her with large, motionless, almond-shaped eyes. She was evidently aware of her beauty and afraid because of it. Her face struck Pierre, and as he hurried along the fence he turned several times to look at her. When he reached the fence and still had not found the people he was looking for, he stopped and looked around.
With the child in his arms he stood out more than before, and a group of Russians, men and women, gathered around him.
"Have you lost someone, my dear fellow? You're of the gentry yourself, aren't you? Whose child is it?" they asked him.
Pierre answered that the child belonged to a woman in a black coat who had been sitting there with her other children, and he asked whether anyone knew where she had gone.
"Why, that must be the Anferovs," said an old deacon, turning to a pockmarked peasant woman. "Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy!" he added in his usual bass.
"The Anferovs? No," said the woman. "They left in the morning. It must be Mary Nikolaevna's or the Ivanovs'!"
"He says 'a woman,' and Mary Nikolaevna is a lady," remarked a house serf.
"Do you know her? She's thin, with long teeth," said Pierre.
"That's Mary Nikolaevna! They went into the garden when these wolves swooped down," said the woman, pointing at the French soldiers.
"O Lord, have mercy!" added the deacon.
"Go over that way, they're there. It's her! She kept on wailing and crying," the woman went on. "It's her. Here, this way!"

But Pierre was not listening to the woman. For some seconds he had been watching intently something that was happening a few steps away. He was looking at the Armenian family and at two French soldiers who had walked up to them. One of them was a nimble little man in a blue coat tied around the waist with a rope. He had a nightcap on his head, and his feet were bare. The other struck Pierre especially. He was a tall, lank, round-shouldered, fair-haired man, slow in his movements, with an idiotic look on his face. He wore a woman's loose frieze gown, blue trousers and big torn Hessian boots. The little barefoot Frenchman in the blue coat went up to the Armenians, said something and at once seized the old man by the legs, and the old man immediately began pulling off his boots. The other, in the frieze gown, stopped in front of the beautiful Armenian girl and stood staring at her, motionless and silent, with his hands in his pockets.

"Here, take the child!" Pierre said to the woman, sharply and in a hurry, handing the little girl to her. "Give her back to them, give her back!" he almost shouted. He set the child, who began to scream, on the ground and looked again at the Frenchman and the Armenian family.

The old man was already sitting barefoot. The little Frenchman had got his second boot and was slapping the two boots together. The old man was saying something in a voice broken by sobs, but Pierre barely caught a glimpse of this. All his attention was on the Frenchman in the frieze gown, who by now had swayed slowly over to the young woman. He took his hands out of his pockets and seized her by the neck.
The beautiful Armenian was still sitting motionless in the same posture, her long lashes lowered, as if she neither saw nor felt what the soldier was doing to her.

Pierre ran the few steps that separated him from the Frenchman. By then the tall marauder in the frieze gown was already tearing off the necklace the young Armenian wore, and the young woman, clutching at her neck, screamed piercingly.
"Leave that woman alone!" Pierre shouted hoarsely in a furious voice. He seized the soldier by his round shoulders and threw him aside.
The soldier fell, got up and ran away. But his comrade threw down the boots, drew his sword and moved threateningly toward Pierre.
"Voyons, pas de bêtises!" * he cried.
* "Look here, no nonsense!"

Pierre was in such a transport of rage that he remembered nothing, and his strength grew tenfold. He rushed at the barefoot Frenchman and, before the man had time to draw his sword, knocked him off his feet and pounded him with his fists. Cries of approval came from the crowd around them. At the same moment a mounted patrol of French Uhlans appeared around the corner. The Uhlans trotted up to Pierre and the Frenchman and surrounded them. Pierre remembered nothing of what happened next. He only remembered beating someone and being beaten, and finally feeling that his hands were tied and that a crowd of French soldiers stood around him searching him.
"Lieutenant, he has a dagger," were the first words Pierre understood.

"Ah, a weapon?" said the officer, and he turned to the barefoot soldier who had been arrested with Pierre. "All right, you can tell all about it at the court-martial." Then he turned to Pierre. "Do you speak French?"

Pierre looked around him with bloodshot eyes and did not answer. His face probably looked terrible, because the officer whispered something, and four more Uhlans left the ranks and placed themselves on either side of Pierre.
"Do you speak French?" the officer asked again, keeping away from Pierre. "Call the interpreter."
A little man in Russian civilian clothes rode out of the ranks. From his clothes and his way of speaking, Pierre knew at once that he was a French salesman from one of the Moscow shops.
"He doesn't look like a common man," said the interpreter, after a searching look at Pierre.
"Ah, he looks very much like an incendiary," remarked the officer. "And ask him who he is," he added.
"Who are you?" asked the interpreter in poor Russian. "You must answer the chief."
"I won't tell you who I am. I am your prisoner — take me!" Pierre suddenly answered in French.
"Ah, ah!" the officer muttered with a frown. "Well then, march!"
A crowd had gathered around the Uhlans. The pockmarked peasant woman with the little girl stood nearest to Pierre, and when the patrol set off she stepped forward.
"Where are they taking you, you poor dear?" she said. "And the little girl, the little girl, what am I to do with her if she's not theirs?" said the woman.
"What does that woman want?" asked the officer.
Pierre felt as if he were drunk. The sight of the little girl he had saved made his elation even greater.

"What does she want?" he murmured. "She's bringing me my daughter, whom I have just saved from the flames," he said. "Good-by!" He had no idea how this pointless lie had slipped out of him. He went along between the French soldiers with resolute, triumphant steps.

The French patrol was one of those that Durosnel had ordered into the various streets of Moscow to put a stop to the pillaging and, above all, to catch the incendiaries. The general opinion among the higher French officers, formed that very day, held that the incendiaries were the cause of the fires. After marching through a number of streets, the patrol arrested five more Russian suspects: a small shopkeeper, two seminary students, a peasant and a house serf, besides several looters. But of all these suspects, Pierre was considered the most suspicious. They were all brought for the night to a large house on the Zubov Rampart that was being used as a guardhouse, and there Pierre was put apart under strict guard.
